questions.question: Define a tourist clause by clause, distinguish the three flows of tourism with their trade logic, and explain why economists classify inbound tourism as an export.
questions.expected_answer: A tourist, on the UN World Tourism Organisation definition, is a person travelling outside his or her usual environment, for less than a year, for leisure, business or other purposes not connected with earning money at the destination. Outside the usual environment excludes commuting and everyday shopping; less than a year excludes migration; not remunerated at the destination excludes taking a job there — a consultant paid by a local firm is a worker, while a conference delegate paid from home is a business tourist. A visitor staying at least one night is a tourist proper; a same-day visitor is a day visitor or excursionist, counted but spending far less. The flows: domestic tourism is residents travelling within their own country — rands circulating at home, supporting jobs but bringing in no new money; inbound tourism is foreigners arriving here; outbound is residents travelling abroad, an import that leaks spending out. Inbound tourism is an export because the foreign visitor spends foreign currency inside our borders on locally produced services — the transaction runs like any export sale except that the customer travels to the product, and the product (the mountain, the reserve, the culture) remains behind to be sold again. Netting inbound earnings against outbound spending gives the tourism balance, which South Africa runs at a surplus.

questions.question: Explain how tourism affects GDP and employment, including the multiplier and the three rings around a lodge, and balance the account with the main costs and leakages.
questions.expected_answer: Tourist spending on accommodation, transport, meals, guiding and crafts is final demand feeding directly into production: before the pandemic tourism contributed about 3 percent of South African GDP directly and 8 to 9 percent with indirect effects. The gap is the multiplier: the lodge buys vegetables, laundry and security locally (indirect ring, firms selling to the lodge), its payroll — receptionists, chefs, guides, housekeepers — forms the direct ring, and all those workers spend wages at the spaza, taxi and salon (induced ring), each round adding income; the chain runs long because tourism's inputs are heavily local. Employment: tourism is labour-intensive — beds, meals and guiding are produced by people — so a rand of tourism demand out-hires a rand of mining; the jobs absorb semi-skilled workers, employ many women and young people, and appear in rural districts where no factory will locate, since a game lodge is an immovable export industry standing in a village. The cost column: externalities such as seasonal crowding, pressure on water and land, litter in fragile places, and cultural commodification; leakages when foreign ownership, imported inputs and overseas-sold packages let much of each rand exit before multiplying; and seasonality that hires in December and retrenches in February. Households, businesses, infrastructure and the state all benefit — wages, revenue, lasting airports and roads, VAT and levies — but a full answer weighs both columns.

questions.question: Describe South Africa's tourism profile including the role of indigenous knowledge systems and their two policy duties, and propose four policy improvements each tied to a named obstacle.
questions.expected_answer: The shop window rests on four pillars: scenery and wildlife (Kruger and the private reserves, the Garden Route, the Drakensberg, Table Mountain, with the Big Five as global calling card); heritage and culture (ten UNESCO World Heritage Sites including Robben Island, the Cradle of Humankind, iSimangaliso and uKhahlamba-Drakensberg, plus township routes, battlefields and winelands); events and business (conference centres, sports tours, festivals — the MICE market); and climate. Indigenous knowledge systems — the accumulated knowledge, practices and expressions of indigenous communities — are an asset in their own right: tracking and rock-art interpretation, traditional healing and plant knowledge, storytelling, beadwork, cuisine and dance, converted into livelihoods through cultural villages, heritage routes and craft markets that earn where gate fees never reach. Two duties attach: authenticity — the culture stays owned and told by its own communities, performed with them, not staged about them — and benefit-sharing — the community, not only the operator, banks the earnings. Policy architecture: the 1996 White Paper (government leads, private sector delivers, communities benefit), the Tourism Act of 2014, South African Tourism funded partly by the one-percent TOMSA levy, grading for quality, and priority status in the National Development Plan. Improvements tied to obstacles: slow visas — extend e-visas to China and India; crime perception — visible policing of tourist routes and a safe airport-to-hotel first hour; scarce, expensive flights — negotiate more direct routes; short skills — train guides, chefs and managers ahead of demand; concentrated benefits — develop and market beyond the Cape-Kruger corridor into township, rural and IKS products; unreliable services — keep electricity and water running, since failure videos undo marketing budgets.
